strengths: Addresses an underexplored but practically important task: audio chaptering for long-form podcasts, lectures, and videos, moving beyond transcript-only text segmentation.

Formalizes and analyzes multiple evaluation protocols, especially the transcript-invariant discrete-time protocol T1, and exposes the lossiness and transcript-dependence of text-space evaluation; the oracle analysis helps quantify the discretization ceiling.

Provides a broad empirical comparison across text-based models, a new audio-only architecture (AudioSeg), and multimodal LLMs, with useful ablations on transcript quality, acoustic feature categories, audio encoders, duration, speaker regime, and non-speech cues.

Audio-only AudioSeg with a Whisper Large encoder achieves strong segmentation performance and outperforms text-based MiniSeg variants in several important settings, supporting the value of acoustic and learned audio representations for chaptering.

Offers actionable empirical findings: pause features drive most hand-crafted acoustic gains, speaker features help multi-speaker content, ASR WER does not directly predict segmentation quality, and joint reference+ASR training improves robustness.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: code and AudioSeg are promised for release, dataset/annotations are described, prompts and hyperparameters are provided, and appendices document feature extraction and alignment details.
The paper is clearly structured and well supported by tables and figures, with transparent reporting of failure modes and limitations.
weaknesses: The central comparison between AudioSeg and text-based baselines may be confounded by encoder strength and domain match: AudioSeg uses a large frozen Whisper encoder trained on massive ASR/YouTube-style data, while text baselines use a much smaller MiniLM sentence encoder. A text baseline with a comparably strong language encoder is missing, so the claim that audio-only segmentation is inherently superior to text-based segmentation is not fully established.

The proposed continuous-time protocol T2 is formalized but not empirically evaluated; the main results rely on T1 with 6-second chunks, so the transcript-invariant evaluation contribution is only partially validated.

Text-based models with audio features depend on forced alignment and sentence segmentation from ASR, which may introduce noise or bias; results could be sensitive to alignment quality and chunk/tolerance choices.

MLLM evaluation is limited to two Qwen models, restricted to videos under 30 minutes due to context limits, and not exhaustively tuned over prompts or strategies; conclusions about MLLM viability remain preliminary.

The study relies on a single English-language dataset (YTSeg) with user-generated chapter boundaries and no inter-annotator agreement or human evaluation of boundary quality, limiting generalizability and validation of the gold standard.

Some conclusions are overstated: AudioSeg does not dominate text-based models at longer durations, and combining all acoustic features only marginally exceeds pause duration alone, so the practical significance of individual feature gains is modest.

The audio-only architecture is largely a composition of existing components (frozen encoder, local transformer, RoFormer), with limited architectural novelty; the stronger contribution is the evaluation and empirical study rather than the model.

There is no comparison to simple pause/silence-based segmentation baselines or strong text segmentation baselines beyond MiniSeg, and chapter title generation is not evaluated despite being part of the MLLM output.

strengths: The paper addresses audio chaptering, an understudied and practically relevant task, and motivates it well in terms of non-linear consumption of long audio and video.

It formalizes a useful taxonomy of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2), making explicit the mismatch between continuous-time chapter boundaries and discrete text-space metrics and proposing transcript-invariant evaluation.

The empirical study is broad, covering text-based segmentation with and without acoustic features, an audio-only AudioSeg architecture, and multimodal LLMs under zero-shot, ICL, chunking, self-cascaded, and LoRA settings.

The analysis yields concrete insights: pause duration is the strongest hand-crafted acoustic feature, speaker features help mainly in multi-speaker content, ASR quality does not directly predict segmentation quality, and joint reference plus ASR training improves robustness.
Reproducibility is generally strong, with detailed hyperparameters, prompts, feature extraction descriptions, dataset annotations, and a stated plan to release code and AudioSeg.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with informative tables and appendices.
weaknesses: The central claim that audio-only segmentation is superior is confounded by model capacity and pretraining: AudioSeg uses Whisper Large, an ASR encoder trained with transcript supervision, while the text baseline MiniSeg uses a much smaller MiniLM encoder. This makes it unclear whether gains come from acoustic cues or ASR-derived linguistic knowledge, and stronger text-only baselines are missing.
Evidence is limited to a single English YouTube dataset (YTSeg), so generalization to other languages, domains, and chaptering conventions remains unverified.

The proposed T2 continuous-time protocol is formalized but not empirically evaluated; the main results rely solely on T1 with a fixed 6-second chunk size, and no sensitivity analysis for chunk duration is provided. The oracle T1 F1 ceiling of roughly 73-81% also signals that the discretized protocol introduces substantial loss.
Chaptering includes title generation, but evaluation only scores boundary placement; there is no human evaluation of chapter quality or title usefulness.

The MLLM conclusions are based on videos under 30 minutes and are sensitive to prompting; the claim that MLLMs are promising is weakly supported relative to the audio-only model, which remains substantially better.

The paper could better disentangle whether Whisper's advantage stems from acoustic structure or from its ASR pretraining, for example by comparing stronger self-supervised speech encoders or text encoders of comparable scale.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and relatively underexplored task, audio chaptering, and provides a systematic comparison of three paradigms: text-based models, an audio-only architecture (AudioSeg), and multimodal LLMs.

It formalizes several evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2/H3, T1, T2) and clearly articulates the mismatch between continuous-time chapter boundaries and text-space segmentation metrics, which is a useful methodological contribution.

The empirical study is broad: it includes encoder ablations, hand-crafted audio feature ablations, duration and speaker-regime stratification, MLLM prompting/fine-tuning variants, and failure analysis.
The paper is generally well-written and reproducible in intent: it provides hyperparameters, prompts, feature-extraction details, and promises to release code, AudioSeg, and annotations.
Several findings are practically useful, such as the weak direct link between ASR WER and segmentation quality, and the targeted benefit of speaker features in multi-speaker content.
weaknesses: The central claim that audio-only segmentation is superior 'beyond transcripts' is confounded by the use of the Whisper Large encoder, which is pretrained with ASR/transcript supervision on large-scale web audio. The weaker performance of HuBERT and other self-supervised/non-ASR encoders suggests that the gains may come largely from ASR-like linguistic representations or domain match, not from acoustic cues that are complementary to transcripts.

The largest claimed acoustic gain comes from pause duration, but pause information can be derived from ASR decoder timestamps without access to the raw audio signal. The paper does not compare against a text-based model augmented with ASR-derived timing/pause features, so it does not establish that the improvement requires acoustic modeling.

Protocol T2 is presented as the most direct and truly transcript-invariant evaluation, but it is never empirically evaluated. All experiments use T1, so the proposed evaluation framework remains only partially validated.

The empirical claims rest on a single dataset (YTSeg) and a single domain (English YouTube), with no multiple-seed variance or statistical significance testing. Many reported F1 differences are small enough that noise could plausibly explain them, making broad claims about audio superiority premature.

The MLLM evaluation is restricted to videos under 30 minutes due to context limits, and the MLLM prompt asks for chapter titles in addition to segmentation while text-based baselines are trained only for segmentation. This makes the cross-paradigm comparison less controlled.

The paper overstates some conclusions, e.g., 'substantially outperforms' and 'audio provides complementary or even superior information to text,' without sufficiently controlling for encoder pretraining, ASR-timestamp-derived features, or dataset/domain effects.

Reproducibility is incomplete in places: train/validation/test split sizes are not reported, inference cost is not discussed, and possible overlap between Whisper's pretraining data and YTSeg is acknowledged but not analyzed.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely under-explored and practically relevant task (audio chaptering) and correctly identifies that prior work has been almost entirely transcript-centric, leaving the role of audio, ASR robustness, and transcript-invariant evaluation unresolved.

The formalization of evaluation protocols is a clear and useful methodological contribution. The R1/H1/H2/H3 text-space vs. T1/T2 time-space taxonomy cleanly exposes the lossy discretization of continuous-time boundaries and the non-comparability of ASR-dependent metrics, and the oracle analysis (Table A7) quantifying the ~73-81% ceiling of text-space protocols is a compelling justification for time-based evaluation.

The empirical study is broad and systematic: three paradigms (text-based, audio-only, MLLMs), multiple encoders, hand-crafted feature ablations, duration/speaker stratification, and cross-domain validation on AMI. The finding that pause duration drives most of the gains while speaker features help specifically in multi-speaker content is well-supported by Tables 4-5 and A4.

Reproducibility is strong: hyperparameters (Tables A12-A14), prompts (Figures A1-A5), feature-extraction details (Appendix G), dataset statistics, and a released toolkit/model are all provided, and the failure analysis of MLLMs (Table A2) is unusually transparent.

The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with informative figures (duration and speaker-proportion curves) and honest discussion of limitations, including the single-dataset and English-only concerns.
weaknesses: The headline claim that audio-only segmentation 'substantially outperforms' text-based approaches is confounded. AudioSeg uses a frozen Whisper Large encoder that was trained on large-scale YouTube audio (a domain match with YTSeg), while the text baseline uses a comparatively small MiniLM sentence encoder. The authors acknowledge the possible domain match, but no controlled comparison with a comparably strong text encoder is provided, so the superiority claim is not cleanly isolated from encoder strength and domain overlap.

Architectural novelty is limited: AudioSeg is essentially MiniSeg's hierarchical design (frozen encoder -> local transformer -> RoFormer document encoder) transplanted to audio, so the main contribution rests on the empirical/evaluation analysis rather than a new modeling idea.

The evaluation-protocol contribution, while valuable, is validated only with MiniSeg variants in Table A10; the protocol comparison would be more convincing if it also demonstrated ranking consistency across the audio-only and MLLM systems that the protocols are meant to unify.

Several central conclusions rest on a single primary dataset (YTSeg), and the AMI cross-domain test uses very small splits (validation/test of 9/4 and 16/16). The generality of the duration/speaker conclusions is therefore uncertain.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided for the main comparisons, despite many small F1 differences (e.g., 1.5-point variations across transcript types) that could fall within noise.

Some findings are close to expected (MLLMs are weak at precise temporal grounding and degrade with long context; longer videos have sparser boundaries), which reduces the incremental surprise beyond the evaluation-protocol contribution.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored task—audio chaptering—and makes a convincing case for moving beyond transcript-centric evaluation.

Formalizes a useful suite of evaluation protocols (R1, H1–H3, T1–T2) that clearly separate transcript-dependent text-space evaluation from transcript-invariant time-space evaluation; this is a valuable methodological contribution for the community.

Provides extensive and well-organized experiments spanning text-based models, audio-only models, and MLLMs, with multiple audio encoders, feature ablations, duration/speaker stratification, and cross-domain validation on AMI.

Reproducibility is strong: the paper releases an evaluation toolkit and AudioSeg, describes feature extraction, hyperparameters, and prompts in detail, and includes failure analyses and protocol sensitivity checks.

The main empirical findings are generally well supported: AudioSeg with Whisper encoders outperforms text-based baselines on YTSeg, pauses provide the largest acoustic feature gain, ASR quality does not directly predict segmentation performance, and MLLMs are limited by context and instruction following but promising on shorter audio.
The paper is clearly written, with thoughtful limitations and risk sections, and the release of annotations and evaluation tooling is likely to facilitate follow-up work.
weaknesses: The central comparison between audio-only and text-based models may not be fully fair: MiniSeg uses a relatively small MiniLM/RoFormer text encoder, while AudioSeg uses a large, powerful Whisper encoder. No fine-tuned large text-only baseline is included, so the claimed superiority of audio-only modeling may partly reflect encoder scale/pretraining rather than modality alone.

The best audio-only model relies on Whisper, an ASR-pretrained encoder that has learned from transcript supervision and likely encodes linguistic structure. This complicates the “beyond transcripts” framing: non-ASR speech encoders such as HuBERT and PE-A-Frame perform substantially worse, suggesting the strongest gains may come from ASR-derived representations rather than purely acoustic cues.

Protocol T1 discretizes audio into 6-second chunks chosen to match average sentence length, which may favor AudioSeg’s native segment resolution. Although T2 and chunk-size sensitivity analyses are reported, the main tables lack statistical significance tests or confidence intervals, making some small differences difficult to interpret.

MLLM experiments are restricted to videos under 30 minutes because of context limits, so conclusions about MLLMs, temporal grounding, and title generation are only partial and do not cover the full dataset distribution.

AudioSeg is largely an engineering combination of existing components (frozen audio encoder, local transformer, RoFormer document encoder), so the architectural novelty is modest; the paper’s primary contribution is empirical/analytical rather than a new modeling technique.

Potential domain match between YTSeg (YouTube videos) and Whisper’s training data is acknowledged but not fully controlled; while the AMI cross-domain results help, the main YTSeg gains may still be somewhat inflated by this overlap.

strengths: Provides a genuinely useful and clearly formalized evaluation-protocol taxonomy (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) that makes explicit two real problems in prior work: ASR-based text-space evaluation (H1) is not transcript-invariant, and projecting continuous-time boundaries onto sentence units is inherently lossy. The oracle experiment quantifying this discretization ceiling (F1≈73–81%) is a concrete and valuable diagnostic.

Broad, well-organized empirical sweep across three paradigms (text-based, audio-only, MLLM), multiple encoders, hand-crafted feature ablations, chunk-size sensitivity, duration/speaker stratification, and a cross-domain check on AMI. The research questions are clearly posed and addressed.

Strong reproducibility: released evaluation toolkit and model, full hyperparameter tables, verbatim prompts, and detailed feature-extraction methodology (pauses, pitch, loudness, speaker features). This is a genuine asset for the community.

Several findings are independently useful and non-obvious, e.g., that pause duration drives most of the acoustic gain when augmenting text models, and that ASR word-error rate does not monotonically predict segmentation quality.
Honest limitations/risks sections and a transparent MLLM failure-mode analysis (missing tags, generation loops, empty chapters, transcript-length ratios).
weaknesses: The headline claim ('beyond transcripts'; transcript-free segmentation is 'superior') is confounded. The only audio-only system that beats the text baselines uses Whisper-Large, a transcript-supervised ASR encoder whose representations are explicitly shaped to encode linguistic content. A genuinely acoustic self-supervised encoder (HuBERT Large, F1=35.58) falls below the best text-based MiniSeg (Ref+ASR_T, F1=40.01), directly contradicting the paper's thesis. The paper notes Whisper 'implicitly captures linguistic structure' in passing, but the abstract and conclusion still overclaim that 'learned audio representations capture structural cues beyond what transcripts provide.'

The cross-paradigm comparison is not apples-to-apples. Text models predict at sentence granularity and are then projected onto the 6s evaluation grid via forced alignment, incurring the discretization loss the paper itself quantifies, whereas AudioSeg is trained and evaluated natively at the 6s resolution. Part of AudioSeg's advantage may therefore be an evaluation-alignment artifact rather than superior segmentation ability, and the reported oracle ceiling (~73–81%) shows text models are systematically handicapped in this setup.

Evidence is narrow relative to the paper's ambition to 'establish a methodological foundation': a single primary English dataset (YTSeg) with user-generated YouTube chapter labels that are noisy and often driven by non-content cues (ads, sponsors, structural markers). The AMI cross-domain validation rests on very few meetings (9/4 and 16/16), limiting generalization claims.

Limited novelty. MiniSeg is prior work; AudioSeg is a straightforward frozen-encoder → local transformer → RoFormer pipeline; T1/T2 are natural 'evaluate in time space' formulations. The contribution is essentially a benchmark/analysis paper rather than a new method or dataset.

Many reported differences are small (e.g., +0.67 F1 from speaker features) and the main tables report no significance tests or confidence intervals, so several conclusions are fragile. The claim that 'ASR quality does not directly predict segmentation performance' rests on only two Whisper variants, and the non-speech-cue ablation (DeepFilterNet) shows only a modest drop (-2.21 F1).

The MLLM analysis is largely a study of failure modes; even the best MLLM configuration (F1=41.30) does not clearly surpass the text baseline, so the takeaways about multimodal LLMs are limited in scope and depth.
